entries: *Entry 69:

Another tussle in the raptor cage. Lost another one from the first generation. Just the Big One left now. She's trouble  clever, calculating, and patient. Doesn't make a sound unless she wants to. I've seen lions like her before, but never with eyes that sharp.
*Entry 72:

First real field test with the Spinosaurus today. More dangerous in water than on land. Moves quiet as a croc until it wants to strike, then the power comes out of nowhere. I advised we limit its enclosure to half the size  the bigger the territory, the harder it is to keep it from testing the fences.
*Entry 75:

The Baryonyx has been less trouble than expected, but don't let that fool anyone. It's patient and prefers fish, but I've seen it size up workers at the water's edge. Reminder: don't trust a mild-mannered carnivore. Hunger changes everything.
*Entry 78:

Hammond insists on having cows ready to feed to the raptors, just to impress the visitors. I've told him again and again it encourages unnatural feeding behaviour, but he accuses me of being too cautious and laughs it off. He's grown more headstrong since he took on Site A.

Proposed we house them in open paddocks, like big cats. I saw the same frustration and pacing in the lions back at the safari park, before we moved them to the new plains enclosure. He listened to me then, but now he refuses. He prefers the look of their cage, aesthetics over sense.
*Entry 80:

The Dilophosaurs are a nuisance. They don't just bite  they spit. Blinds you, burns your skin, leaves you half-conscious for the pack to finish off. Their range is better than I'd guessed, ten feet at least. We're revising containment procedures immediately.
*Entry 83:

Placed an order for thermal imaging goggles to monitor the Dilophosaurs. They keep bloody vanishing into the undergrowth. Ordered five units. Hammond immediately requisitioned most of them to hand out to guests. Should arrive just after full opening, if the supply chain holds.
*Entry 84:

The men at Site B finally bothered to send through their tranquiliser recommendations. I've copied them into my blue notebook. They suggest restraining the animal first, then darting it with a morphine-based formula mixed with trace amounts of redstone.
Interesting idea, but I'd like to see them try that on Rexy. Restraining her before the dart goes in sounds like a good way to get yourself killed.
*Entry 86:

Microraptors again. They slip through gaps like shadows, climb anything, and glide off before you can blink. We'll need full roofed enclosures  aviaries, not paddocks. If they ever get into the main park, guests won't spot them until it's too late.
*Entry 88:

Pachycephalosaurs slammed one of the steel gates hard enough to dent it. They're not just bone-headed; they're relentless once they fixate on something. Recommend doubled bracing and reinforced hinges on all gates in their paddocks.
*Entry 89:
The door on Feeder number 27 jammed  looks like one of the sauropods stepped on the mechanism. Another thing to fix.
Meanwhile, the raptors tried another breakout. All were sedated and returned, though one worker was injured in the process. The enclosure security is becoming a serious concern.
Also, I'm nearly out of cigarettes.
*Entry 90:

El Niño is scheduled for next year. Hammond looked surprised when I told him. Didn't realise his tropical paradise wasn't exempt from the weather. Fish stocks will likely collapse. That'll be a bigger problem for the Site B spineys than anything over here, but it'll ripple through the food chains all the same.
*Entry 91:
Looks like the last storm before the El Niño is going to be brutal. Ordered extra sedatives and emergency feed stock. If the generators fail in that weather, we're all in for a rough time.
*Entry 95:
The Ankylosaurs are docile enough, but if spooked, their tails can smash concrete. Workers keep underestimating them because they're herbivores. Herbivore doesn't mean harmless.
*Entry 98:

Maiasaur herds keep spooking at shadows. When one bolts, the rest follow. A stampede of forty tons of flesh is harder to stop than any predator. We'll need wide, open paddocks with minimal choke points, or else someone's going to get trampled.
